resource_name: Identify the Care Setting Before Choosing the Route
primary_evidence: description 'Medicare' in "Neglect looks the same from the outside and is addressed by completely different systems depending on WHERE it" @ manual-review-action:elder_care_protection|elder_neglect|US|setting_identification
source_text:
Identify the Care Setting Before Choosing the Route
Neglect looks the same from the outside and is addressed by completely different systems depending on WHERE it is happening. Answer this first. (1) IN THE OLDER ADULT'S OWN HOME, with care provided by family or informally: the route is Adult Protective Services plus caregiver support services -- and note that a large share of neglect in this setting is a caregiver capacity failure rather than malice, which changes the correct intervention entirely toward respite, home-delivered meals, and in-home services. (2) IN THE HOME, with care provided by a licensed HOME CARE OR HOME HEALTH AGENCY: APS plus a complaint to the agency's state licensing body, plus -- if the agency is Medicare-certified -- the state survey agency, since Medicare-certified home health agencies are subject to federal conditions of participation and are listed with quality data on Care Compare. (3) IN AN ASSISTED LIVING FACILITY OR ADULT FAMILY HOME: state licensing plus the Ombudsman -- see the Assisted Living Complaint pipeline. (4) IN A CERTIFIED NURSING FACILITY: the state survey agency under federal rules -- see the Nursing Home Abuse pipeline. (5) SELF-NEGLECT, where the older adult is not caring for themselve
Use when intake resolves to elder neglect and this source-backed route matches the facts.
Choose from 1 reviewed source-backed route option.

resource_name: Report inaccessible federal technology or information
primary_evidence: description 'attorney' in "Section 508 requires federal agencies to make their electronic and information technology (ICT) — websites, so" @ manual-review-action:disability_services|federal_technology_accessibility|US|report_inaccessible_federal_technology
source_text:
Report inaccessible federal technology or information
Section 508 requires federal agencies to make their electronic and information technology (ICT) — websites, software, hardware, documents, and multimedia — accessible to people with disabilities, both employees and members of the public. It applies to ICT that agencies develop, procure, maintain, or use. Enforcement uses the Rehabilitation Act's §505 remedies: after exhausting administrative remedies, individuals may bring a private action for injunctive/equitable relief and attorney's fees (no compensatory or punitive damages). It is distinct from §504 in that it sets specific technical standards for federal technology. Filing Deadlines: A complaint may be filed with the noncompliant federal agency; the agency applies its §504 federally-conducted-program complaint procedures (generally a 180-day filing window under those procedures). Section 508 obligations for ICT procured 6+ months after the Access Board's final standards apply. Recent amendments: The 2017 'Section 508 ICT Refresh' final rule (effective March 17, 2017) remains the current standard; federal agencies have been required to comply with the revised standards since January 18, 2018 (subject to safe-harbor provisions).
Use this when a federal agency's electronic or information technology is inaccessible.

source_text:
SUPPORT for Patients and Communities Act (2018)
The SUPPORT Act is a wide-ranging 2018 law (over 70 provisions) that expanded access to opioid and substance use disorder treatment across Medicaid, Medicare, and public health programs. Section 1012 and Section 5052 create a temporary Medicaid 'IMD exception,' allowing federal payment for SUD treatment services delivered in Institutions for Mental Diseases for eligible adults, including up to 30 days of coverage per year for enrollees aged 21–64. It mandates Medicaid prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) checks before prescribing controlled substances, expands coverage for opioid treatment programs and medication-assisted treatment under Medicare, and requires opioid and SUD screening at Medicare wellness visits. The law also funds recovery housing best practices, loan repayment for SUD workforce, comprehensive opioid recovery centers, and expands telehealth-delivered treatment access, particularly for medication-assisted treatment.

Federal Resident Rights Under the Nursing Home Reform Act
If this facility is Medicare- or Medicaid-CERTIFIED -- which most nursing homes and skilled nursing facilities are -- a federal rulebook applies that does NOT apply to assisted living or adult family homes. THE FEDERAL RIGHTS THAT ARE ENFORCEABLE: to be free from abuse, neglect, misappropriation of property, corporal punishment, and INVOLUNTARY SECLUSION; to be free from PHYSICAL OR CHEMICAL RESTRAINTS imposed for discipline or staff convenience rather than to treat medical symptoms -- antipsychotic medication given to a resident without a qualifying diagnosis is a chemical restraint and is one of the most heavily cited violations nationally; to a comprehensive assessment and a care plan the resident participates in developing; to the services necessary to attain and maintain the HIGHEST PRACTICABLE physical, mental, and psychosocial well-being, which means decline that was avoidable is itself a violation; to manage personal funds and receive an accounting; to voice grievances WITHOUT retaliation; to visitors including

source_text:
Use vocational-rehabilitation programs or Rehabilitation Act rights
The Rehabilitation Act of 1973 is the foundational federal disability rights statute. Title I authorizes the federal-state Vocational Rehabilitation (VR) program, funding state agencies that help people with disabilities prepare for, obtain, and keep employment. Other key provisions include Section 501 (federal employment), Section 503 (federal contractors), Section 504 (federally funded programs), Section 508 (federal ICT accessibility), Title II (disability research via NIDILRR), and Title VII (independent living). It predates and heavily influenced the ADA. Filing Deadlines: VR applicants/recipients may pursue mediation and an impartial due-process hearing through the state VR agency (timeframes set by state VR procedures) and receive assistance from the Client Assistance Program. Section 504-based discrimination complaints follow the applicable funding agency's ~180-day administrative deadline (Title VI remedies). Recent amendments: The most recent statutory revision of the Rehabilitation Act came in 2014 via WIOA (Pub. L. 113-128), which amended Title I VR and moved NIDILRR (Title II) and the Independent Living programs (Title VII) from the Dept. of Education to the Administra
Use this for vocational-rehabilitation services, disability employment programs, or disability discrimination covered by the Rehabilitation Act.

source_text:
Check disability-discrimination rights and enforcement options
The ADA is the nation's most comprehensive civil rights law prohibiting discrimination against people with disabilities. It bars discrimination in employment (Title I), in state and local government services and programs (Title II), and in privately operated public accommodations (Title III), and mandates accessible telecommunications (Title IV). The 2008 ADA Amendments Act broadened the definition of 'disability' to reverse restrictive Supreme Court interpretations, directing that the term be construed broadly in favor of coverage. The statute requires reasonable accommodations/modifications and accessibility unless doing so imposes undue hardship or fundamentally alters a program. Filing Deadlines: Title I (employment): file a charge with the EEOC within 180 days of the discriminatory act, extended to 300 days where a state/local fair-employment agency also covers the conduct. Title II: complaints to DOJ generally within 180 days of the alleged discrimination (transportation-related Title II complaints to FTA within 180 days). Title III: no fixed federal administrative filing deadline; private suits borrow the analogous state personal-injury statute of limitations (typically 2-4 
Use this when disability discrimination or an accessibility barrier may involve employment, public services, or public accommodations.

source_text:
Paid In-Home Care -- Agency Licensing, Federal Conditions, and the Service Plan
Where care is paid for and provided by an agency, there is a regulator with authority over that agency, and most families never contact it. TWO DIFFERENT REGIMES: (1) MEDICARE-CERTIFIED HOME HEALTH AGENCIES are subject to federal Conditions of Participation, are surveyed by the state survey agency, and are published with quality and patient-experience data on Medicare Care Compare. Federal requirements include a comprehensive assessment, an individualized plan of care, patient rights including the right to be free from abuse and neglect and to voice grievances without retaliation, and a duty to investigate complaints. Complaints go to the state survey agency and can result in federal enforcement. (2) STATE-LICENSED HOME CARE, PERSONAL CARE, AND HOMEMAKER AGENCIES are governed entirely by state licensing rules covering background checks, training hours, supervision, service plans, and visit documentation. Complaints go to the state licensing office. WHAT TO REQUEST IN WRITING: the SERVICE PLAN or plan of care, which states exactly what was to be provided and how often; the VISIT AND TASK RECORDS or electronic visit verification data, which show whether scheduled visits actually occu

primary_evidence: description 'prescription' in "The Ryan Haight Act amended the Controlled Substances Act to combat illegal online pharmacies by generally req" @ lines:518-545
before_category: Federal statute — Requires an in-person medical evaluation before prescribing controlled substances via telemedicine/internet, subject to ongoing DEA telehealth flexibilities
source_text:
Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Consumer Protection Act (2008)
The Ryan Haight Act amended the Controlled Substances Act to combat illegal online pharmacies by generally requiring practitioners to conduct at least one in-person medical evaluation of a patient before prescribing controlled substances, with an exception for qualifying 'practice of telemedicine' circumstances. This protects patients from unsafe, unverified online prescribing while still allowing legitimate telehealth-based care under defined conditions. Since the COVID-19 public health emergency, DEA and HHS have repeatedly suspended the in-person evaluation requirement through a series of temporary telemedicine flexibility extensions, allowing prescribers to issue Schedule II-V controlled substance prescriptions (including buprenorphine for opioid use disorder via audio-only telemedicine) without a prior in-person visit. As of the most recent (fourth) extension issued December 31, 2025, these flexibilities remain in effect through December 31, 2026, alongside two DEA/HHS final rules (effective December 31, 2025) creating a permanent pathway for telemedicine-based buprenorphine prescribing and continuity of care for VA patients.

primary_evidence: label 'mental health' in "Federal statute — Requires parity between mental health/substance use disorder benefits and medical/surgical b" @ lines:434-461
before_category: Federal statute — Requires parity between mental health/substance use disorder benefits and medical/surgical benefits in group health plans and insurance
source_text:
Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA) — as applied to SUD benefits
MHPAEA requires that group health plans and insurers offering mental health or substance use disorder (SUD) benefits provide those benefits with financial requirements (copays, deductibles) and treatment limitations (visit limits, prior authorization) no more restrictive than those applied to medical/surgical benefits. It bans separate, more restrictive annual or lifetime dollar limits on SUD treatment compared with medical care. As amended by the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021, plans must perform and document comparative analyses of non-quantitative treatment limitations (NQTLs, e.g., prior authorization or network adequacy standards) and provide them to regulators on request within 45 days if deficient. Plans found non-compliant must notify all enrollees within 7 days of a final determination. This law is central to ensuring people can access SUD treatment (including inpatient rehab, outpatient counseling, and medication-assisted treatment) on par with physical health coverage.

resource_name: Building the Money Trail and Documenting Undue Influence
primary_evidence: description 'attorney' in "EXPLOITATION IS PROVEN BY DOCUMENTS, NOT BY IMPRESSIONS. WHAT TO GATHER, AND REQUEST IT IN WRITING: bank and b" @ manual-review-action:elder_care_protection|elder_financial_exploitation|US|money_trail
source_text:
Building the Money Trail and Documenting Undue Influence
EXPLOITATION IS PROVEN BY DOCUMENTS, NOT BY IMPRESSIONS. WHAT TO GATHER, AND REQUEST IT IN WRITING: bank and brokerage statements going back at least two years -- longer if the pattern is older; cancelled checks front AND BACK, since the endorsement shows who actually took the money; wire transfer and ACH records; ATM and card transaction detail with locations; signature cards and any changes to account ownership with the DATES those changes were made; beneficiary designation changes with dates; the deed history from the county recorder for any real property; loan and reverse mortgage documents; and any power of attorney, will, or trust amendment with its execution date and the notary's identity. THE DATES ARE THE CASE. Line the financial changes up against a timeline of the older adult's health, cognition, hospitalizations, and the suspected person's arrival in their life. THE RECOGNIZED INDICATORS OF UNDUE INFLUENCE, which courts weigh: isolation of the older adult from family and prior advisors; a new or intensified relationship coinciding with the transfers; changes made in haste or in secret; use of a new attorney or notary chosen by the suspected person; transfers inconsisten
Use when intake resolves to elder financial exploitation and this route matches the facts.
Choose from 1 reviewed source-backed route option.

resource_name: Prevention -- Trusted Contacts, Monitoring, and Structural Safeguards
primary_evidence: description 'ATTORNEY' in "Once the immediate loss is addressed, close the specific door that was used -- exploitation frequently recurs " @ manual-review-action:elder_care_protection|elder_financial_exploitation|US|prevention
source_text:
Prevention -- Trusted Contacts, Monitoring, and Structural Safeguards
Once the immediate loss is addressed, close the specific door that was used -- exploitation frequently recurs through the same opening, often with a different person. THE STRUCTURAL SAFEGUARDS, in rough order of value: (1) A TRUSTED CONTACT PERSON on every bank and brokerage account -- someone the institution may contact if it suspects exploitation or cannot reach the account holder. This is now standard for brokerage accounts under FINRA rules and widely available at banks. It costs nothing and does not give the contact any authority over the account. (2) TRANSACTION ALERTS to a second person for withdrawals, transfers, and address changes above a set threshold. (3) READ-ONLY VIEW ACCESS for a trusted family member -- visibility without control, which is the right level for most families and is rarely offered. (4) A CAREFULLY DRAFTED DURABLE POWER OF ATTORNEY executed while capacity is intact, naming a trustworthy agent, with a co-agent or a required periodic accounting to a third party built in. A POA is a protection when drafted well and the primary instrument of abuse when drafted carelessly -- see the Power of Attorney Abuse pipeline. (5) A SECURITY FREEZE at all three credit 
Use when intake resolves to elder financial exploitation and this route matches the facts.
Choose from 1 reviewed source-backed route option.

source_text:
FTC Consumer Response Center: 877-382-4357 | CFPB: 855-411-2372 | Your state AG consumer protection division -- see jurisdiction table
Every state has an Unfair and Deceptive Acts and Practices (UDAP) statute, and these are frequently stronger than federal law for an individual: many provide statutory minimum damages, multiple damages, and mandatory attorney fee-shifting, which is what makes a small-dollar case economically viable for a lawyer to take. THE STRUCTURAL POINT: you do not have to prove the seller intended to deceive you under most UDAP statutes -- you generally have to prove the practice was deceptive or unfair and that you were harmed. That is a materially lower bar than common-law fraud, which typically requires proof of intent, and choosing the wrong theory is a common self-inflicted defeat. SPECIFIC RESCISSION RIGHTS WORTH CHECKING IMMEDIATELY: the FTC Cooling-Off Rule gives 3 business days to cancel certain sales of $25 or more made at your home, workplace, or a temporary location; the Truth in Lending Act gives 3 business days to rescind certain loans secured by your principal dwelling, extended to 3 YEARS if required disclosures were never properly given; and many states add their own cancellation windows for specific industries. source_text:
Involuntary Discharge or Transfer -- Notice, Grounds, and the Hearing Clock
IF A DISCHARGE OR TRANSFER NOTICE HAS BEEN ISSUED, THIS IS THE MOST URGENT ENTRY IN THIS DOSSIER AND IT SHOULD BE ACTED ON TODAY. Most states require the facility to give written advance notice -- commonly 30 days, shorter in emergencies -- stating the specific reason, the effective date, the proposed destination, and the resident's right to challenge. A NOTICE THAT OMITS THE SPECIFIC REASON OR THE APPEAL RIGHTS IS DEFECTIVE, and defective notice is itself a ground to stop the discharge. PERMITTED GROUNDS ARE LIMITED in most states to: nonpayment after reasonable notice and opportunity to pay; the resident's needs exceeding what the facility is licensed and staffed to provide; a documented danger to the resident or others; or facility closure. NOT permitted: discharge because the resident or family complained (retaliation, prohibited in nearly every state); because the resident converted from private pay to Medicaid where the facility accepts Medicaid; because the resident is difficult; or because care needs increased in ways the facility could accommodate but prefers not to. primary_evidence: label 'SUD' in "Federal regulation — Confidentiality protections for SUD treatment records, realigned with HIPAA Privacy Rule " @ lines:462-473
before_category: Federal regulation — Confidentiality protections for SUD treatment records, realigned with HIPAA Privacy Rule under a 2024 final rule
source_text:
42 CFR Part 2 — Confidentiality of Substance Use Disorder Patient Records (2024 Final Rule)
42 CFR Part 2 protects the confidentiality of patient records from federally assisted substance use disorder treatment programs, generally requiring patient consent before providers can disclose SUD treatment information, and barring use of such records to prosecute patients absent consent or a qualifying court order. The 2024 Final Rule (issued February 8, 2024, published February 16, 2024) more closely aligns Part 2 with the HIPAA Privacy Rule, permitting a single patient consent to cover future uses/disclosures for treatment, payment, and health care operations (replacing prior disclosure-by-disclosure consent requirements), while preserving Part 2's heightened bar against using records in legal proceedings against patients. It also extends HIPAA breach notification requirements and civil/criminal penalties to Part 2 violations, giving patients stronger enforcement backing and clearer rights to request records and restrictions. This makes it easier for care teams to coordinate SUD treatment with other medical care while maintaining strong privacy protections.

resource_name: Involuntary Transfer or Discharge -- Limited Grounds and a Very Short Hearing Clock
primary_evidence: description 'Medicaid' in "Federal law permits a certified facility to transfer or discharge a resident against their wishes ONLY on enum" @ manual-review-action:elder_care_protection|nursing_home_abuse|US|involuntary_discharge
source_text:
Involuntary Transfer or Discharge -- Limited Grounds and a Very Short Hearing Clock
Federal law permits a certified facility to transfer or discharge a resident against their wishes ONLY on enumerated grounds: the transfer is necessary for the resident's welfare and the facility cannot meet their needs; the resident's health has improved so the facility is no longer needed; the safety or health of individuals in the facility is endangered; the resident has failed, after reasonable and appropriate notice, to pay; or the facility ceases to operate. NOT PERMITTED: discharge because the resident converted from private pay to Medicaid; because the resident or family complained; because the resident is difficult, has dementia-related behaviors the facility is required to manage, or requires more staff attention. 'DUMPING' -- refusing to readmit a resident after a hospital stay -- is a transfer subject to these same rules and to the facility's bed-hold and readmission obligations. THE NOTICE MUST BE WRITTEN, generally 30 DAYS in advance, and must state the specific reason, the effective date, the location of the proposed transfer, the right to appeal, and contact information for the Ombudsman and the protection and advocacy agency. A NOTICE MISSING THESE ELEMENTS IS DEFE
Use when intake resolves to nursing home abuse and this involuntary discharge route matches the person's facts.

source_text:
Controlled Substances Act
The Controlled Substances Act (CSA) is the core federal law regulating the manufacture, distribution, dispensing, and possession of controlled substances, including the medications used to treat substance use disorder (e.g., methadone, buprenorphine, naltrexone). It establishes five drug schedules (I-V) based on medical use and abuse potential, sets registration requirements for practitioners and pharmacies who prescribe or dispense controlled substances, and defines criminal penalties for unlawful manufacture, distribution, or possession. For people in SUD treatment, the CSA governs who may legally prescribe medications for opioid use disorder and under what registration and recordkeeping conditions, and its registration/telemedicine provisions (21 U.S.C. §§ 823, 829, 831) intersect directly with the Ryan Haight Act and the MAT Act's waiver elimination. It also underlies DEA's authority over prescription drug monitoring, take-back programs, and diversion control efforts central to the opioid crisis response.

source_text:
Good Samaritan overdose protections (state laws) and federal Good Samaritan Health Professionals Act
Overdose 'Good Samaritan' laws — which protect individuals who call 911 to report a drug overdose from certain drug possession prosecution — exist only at the state level; all 50 states and D.C. have some form of Good Samaritan or overdose immunity law, but there is no equivalent overarching federal overdose Good Samaritan statute. Separately, a bill titled the 'Good Samaritan Health Professionals Act' (most recently reintroduced as H.R. 1876 in the 115th Congress, 2017-2018, and again as H.R. 2819 in the 118th Congress, 2023) would provide civil liability protection to licensed health professionals who volunteer across state lines during a federally declared disaster. This bill relates to disaster-response liability for volunteer clinicians generally, not specifically to SUD overdose response, and — based on available research — has not been enacted into law in any Congress in which it has been introduced. The citation 'Public Law 115-292' provided in the source request does not correspond to this bill.

primary_evidence: description 'attorney' in "THE CLAIMS AVAILABLE, and they are usually pleaded together: CONVERSION for money or property taken; BREACH OF" @ manual-review-action:elder_care_protection|elder_financial_exploitation|US|civil_recovery
source_text:
Civil Recovery -- Void Transfers, Constructive Trusts, and Enhanced Elder Remedies
THE CLAIMS AVAILABLE, and they are usually pleaded together: CONVERSION for money or property taken; BREACH OF FIDUCIARY DUTY where the person held a power of attorney, trusteeship, guardianship, conservatorship, or payee role; UNDUE INFLUENCE and LACK OF CAPACITY to set aside deeds, transfers, beneficiary changes, wills, and trust amendments; UNJUST ENRICHMENT and CONSTRUCTIVE TRUST to reach assets the money was converted into, including real property purchased with the funds; FRAUDULENT TRANSFER where assets have since been moved to a third party to defeat recovery; and, in many states, a STATUTORY ELDER FINANCIAL ABUSE CLAIM carrying enhanced or multiple damages, attorney FEE-SHIFTING, and sometimes a presumption shifting the burden to the transferee where a confidential relationship existed. ASK SPECIFICALLY WHETHER YOUR STATE HAS THE ENHANCED STATUTORY REMEDY -- it is frequently what makes the case economically viable for an attorney to take. PRESERVATION IS THE PRACTICAL PROBLEM: money spent is generally gone, so ask early about a PREJUDGMENT ATTACHMENT, a lis pendens on real property, a temporary restraining order freezing accounts, or an injunction against further transfers
Use when intake resolves to elder financial exploitation and this route matches the facts.

Caregiver Capacity -- The Services That Prevent Neglect From Recurring
A substantial share of neglect in home settings is a caregiver who is overwhelmed, unwell, unsupported, or simply unable to provide the level of care now required -- not someone who intends harm. Where that is the picture, enforcement alone does not fix it and frequently makes it worse. THE SERVICES TO ASK FOR BY NAME, ALL FREE OR LOW-COST: (1) The AREA AGENCY ON AGING, reachable at 800-677-1116, which conducts assessments and coordinates the entire Older Americans Act service set. (2) The NATIONAL FAMILY CAREGIVER SUPPORT PROGRAM, which funds RESPITE CARE, caregiver counseling, training, and supplemental services -- respite is the single most effective intervention for caregiver-capacity neglect and is chronically underused. (3) HOME-DELIVERED MEALS and congregate nutrition programs. (4) PERSONAL CARE, HOMEMAKER, CHORE, and ADULT DAY SERVICES. (5) MEDICAID HOME AND COMMUNITY-BASED SERVICES waivers, which in most states fund substantial in-home care as an alternative to institutional placement, and which in many states allow a FAMILY MEMBER TO BE PAID as the caregiver through self-directed or consumer-directed options -- ask about this explicitly, it exists in most states and is ra

source_text:
DATA 2000 / Mainstreaming Addiction Treatment (MAT) Act (2023)
Section 1262 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 (the MAT Act) eliminated the federal requirement that practitioners obtain a special DEA 'X-waiver' (DATA-Waiver) before prescribing buprenorphine to treat opioid use disorder. Effective immediately upon enactment (December 29, 2022) and implemented by DEA/SAMHSA guidance on January 12, 2023, any practitioner with a standard DEA registration that includes Schedule III authority can now prescribe buprenorphine for OUD, without a separate waiver application or a cap on the number of patients they may treat. This significantly lowers barriers to office-based opioid treatment, allowing more primary care physicians, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants to prescribe this life-saving medication. A related but separate provision (Section 1263, the MATE Act) added a one-time 8-hour substance use disorder training requirement for new or renewing DEA registrants, effective June 27, 2023.

Reporting Financial Exploitation -- Four Bodies, None of Which Notifies the Others
FILE ALL OF THESE. They serve different functions and none reliably forwards to the others. (1) ADULT PROTECTIVE SERVICES investigates exploitation of a vulnerable adult, can arrange protective services, and can petition or refer for a protective order or guardianship where the older adult cannot protect themselves. Any person may report in every state, anonymously, with good faith immunity. (2) LOCAL LAW ENFORCEMENT -- financial exploitation is a crime in every state, frequently under a dedicated vulnerable adult statute with enhanced penalties. Ask for the report number; you will need it for the financial institution, for credit disputes, and for any restitution claim. A police report is also what many institutions require before reversing transactions. (3) THE DOJ NATIONAL ELDER FRAUD HOTLINE at 833-372-8311 provides case managers who help victims report to the right agencies and follow up -- it is free and it is the single best routing resource in this pipeline. (4) FEDERAL AND REGULATORY: the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov; the FBI's IC3 for anything involving the internet, wire transfers, or cryptocurrency; the CFPB for banks and consumer financial products; FINRA and the state s

source_text:
State Licensing Complaint -- The Only Route With Authority Over the License
The licensing agency is the only body that can fine the facility, impose conditions, suspend admissions, or revoke the license. Everything else -- the Ombudsman, APS, a lawyer -- routes around the license rather than at it. FILING IS FREE, REQUIRES NO ATTORNEY, AND MAY GENERALLY BE DONE ANONYMOUSLY, though a named complainant can usually receive the outcome and appeal a closure. WHAT MAKES A COMPLAINT GET INVESTIGATED RATHER THAN SCREENED OUT: (1) State the LICENSE RULE you believe was violated, not just the harm -- staffing ratios, medication administration and storage, resident assessment and the negotiated service agreement, food service, call system response, incident reporting, background checks, training hours, physical plant. Get the rule numbers from your state's residential care regulations, which are published free online. (2) Give DATES, TIMES, and NAMES. 'They neglect her' is screened out; 'On these three dates the call light went unanswered for over 45 minutes, witnessed by these people' is investigated. (3) Attach photographs, the care plan or negotiated service agreement, medication records, and any written communication with the facility. (4) Say explicitly whether

DOL Wage & Hour Division -- Caribbean District Office (Puerto Rico)
Enforces federal FLSA and FMLA for Puerto Rico. PR minimum wage ($10.50/hr) exceeds federal floor -- PR DOL and UAD enforce local wages; WHD enforces FLSA overtime and FMLA. PROMESA (2016) affects overtime salary threshold in PR (lower than mainland threshold applies). FMLA: employers with 50+ employees, 12 weeks unpaid. PR also has its own sick/vacation leave laws (Law 180-1998 -- mandatory vacation leave; Law 139-1968 -- sick leave): these are enforced by PR DOL, not WHD. Key industries: tourism and hospitality, pharmaceutical manufacturing (major PR sector), healthcare, retail, and agricultural workers (MSPA applies).

before_category: Federal statute — Establishes national framework for opioid/SUD prevention, treatment, recovery, and Plans of Safe Care for substance-exposed infants
source_text:
Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act (CARA) of 2016
CARA is the foundational 2016 federal law responding to the opioid crisis, funding prevention, treatment, and recovery programs and expanding access to naloxone and medication-assisted treatment. It requires states receiving federal child protective services grants to develop 'Plans of Safe Care' for infants born affected by substance use, withdrawal symptoms, or Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder, addressing the health and treatment needs of both infant and caregiver. It expands first responder access to overdose-reversal drugs and supports veterans', women's, and family-focused addiction treatment initiatives. It also addresses collateral consequences of addiction, such as reentry and employment barriers for people in recovery. The law does not create an individual right to sue but conditions state grant funding on compliance.

resource_name: Get accessible voting help or report a voting-access barrier
primary_evidence: description 'litigation' in "The Help America Vote Act of 2002 reformed federal election administration after the 2000 election. For voters" @ manual-review-action:disability_services|accessible_voting|US|get_accessible_voting_help
source_text:
Get accessible voting help or report a voting-access barrier
The Help America Vote Act of 2002 reformed federal election administration after the 2000 election. For voters with disabilities, HAVA Title III requires that each polling place have at least one accessible voting system that allows private and independent voting (including for the blind and visually impaired), sets minimum standards for voting systems, and provides funds to states to improve accessibility. It created the Election Assistance Commission (EAC) as a clearinghouse and standards body. DOJ enforces HAVA's requirements through litigation, and states must maintain administrative complaint procedures under Section 402. ⚠ FATAL DEADLINES: HAVA Section 402 requires each state to establish a uniform, nondiscriminatory administrative complaint procedure; states set the filing timeframes (many require the state to make a final determination within 90 days of filing). HAVA itself does not set a single federal filing deadline; DOJ may bring enforcement actions in federal court. Recent amendments: HAVA (2002) remains the operative statute as of July 2026; no major reauthorization has replaced it. The EAC continues to update Voluntary Voting System Guidelines (VVSG 2.0 adopted 2021)
Use this when voting equipment, polling places, registration, or election information is inaccessible.

primary_evidence: description 'HEALTHCARE' in "Neglect is proven clinically far more often than it is proven by testimony, and a medical evaluation creates a" @ manual-review-action:elder_care_protection|elder_neglect|US|medical_documentation
source_text:
Medical Documentation -- The Clinical Record That Makes a Neglect Case
Neglect is proven clinically far more often than it is proven by testimony, and a medical evaluation creates a dated, neutral record that no later dispute can erase. GET A MEDICAL EVALUATION AND ASK THAT THE FINDINGS BE DOCUMENTED SPECIFICALLY. What clinicians can document that a family cannot: weight trajectory against prior recorded weights; laboratory evidence of dehydration and malnutrition; pressure injury staging, location, and whether the presentation is consistent with the reported care; skin condition and hygiene; medication levels showing doses were not given; untreated infection; fracture patterns; and whether observed findings are consistent or INCONSISTENT with the caregiver's explanation -- that last determination is the single most probative clinical finding in neglect cases. HEALTHCARE PROVIDERS ARE MANDATORY REPORTERS in every state, so a clinical visit frequently generates an APS report independently of yours, from a source agencies weight heavily. REQUEST THE RECORDS: under HIPAA the older adult, or their personal representative, has a right of access to the designated record set, generally within 30 days, at a reasonable cost-based fee, and access cannot be cond
Use when intake resolves to elder neglect and this source-backed route matches the facts.

Enforces PR Law 100 of 1959 (anti-discrimination in employment) -- provides DOUBLE damages for discrimination (more favorable than federal law in some respects). SOL: 1 year for PR Law 100 civil action in PR courts; 180 days to UAD administrative complaint (FEPA); 300 days if dual-filing with EEOC. BILINGUAL: UAD serves in Spanish. PR Law 100 does not have a minimum employee threshold -- covers all employers. Double damages are presumed under PR Law 100 (employer must rebut with just cause).

ANY PERSON CAN REPORT SUSPECTED ABUSE, NEGLECT, OR FINANCIAL EXPLOITATION OF A VULNERABLE ADULT IN EVERY STATE. You do not need to be a mandatory reporter, a professional, a relative, or certain. WHAT APS DOES THAT LICENSING DOES NOT: APS investigates harm to the PERSON and can arrange protective services, emergency placement, and referral for guardianship or law enforcement action.
